faqs.q: What is the best pet insurance in 2026?
faqs.a: There is no single best pet insurance - the honest answer depends on which published fact you care about. Lemonade publishes the lowest starting price (from $10/month), Spot publishes the fastest claim payment (48 hours or less, based on Spot admin data 2019-2024) and Fetch publishes the most detailed pricing (breed-by-breed averages with a stated methodology). Compare quotes for your own pet on each official site, because advertised prices are quoted under different deductible, limit and reimbursement conditions.

faqs.q: Which pet insurance is cheapest?
faqs.a: The lowest published starting prices are Lemonade at $10/month for dogs and cats, Spot at $15/month for dogs and $9/month for cats, and Fetch, which does not publish an entry price but publishes averages of $35/month for dogs and $22/month for cats. These figures are not directly comparable: Spot's price assumes an 80% reimbursement rate, a $500 deductible and a $2,500 annual limit for a specific dog in ZIP 32009, while Fetch's average assumes a $10,000 annual limit, a $300 deductible and 80% reimbursement. Your real price comes from a quote on the brand's official site.

faqs.q: Is there a real pet insurance promo code?
faqs.a: Not from these three brands. Their official sitemaps were checked on 2026-09-25 and none contains a promo code or coupon page. The discounts that do exist on the official sites are Lemonade's multi-pet, bundle and annual-payment discounts, Spot's 10% multi-pet discount and its group/employee discount, and Fetch's 10% military discount plus Fetch Deals member savings. Third-party coupon sites are not a source we use.

faqs.q: How long are pet insurance waiting periods?
faqs.a: Published waiting periods: Lemonade 14 days for illnesses and 30 days for orthopedic conditions (preventative package benefits start the day after purchase); Spot typically 14 days, with state-specific variations detailed in its sample policy; Fetch up to 15 days for accident and illness coverage. Coverage for anything that shows signs before those periods end counts as pre-existing.

faqs.q: Does pet insurance cover pre-existing conditions?
faqs.a: No. All three brands state that pre-existing conditions are not covered. Spot additionally publishes that a curable condition which has been symptom-free and treatment-free for 180 days is no longer considered pre-existing and can become eligible. Fetch counts anything that occurred or showed clinical signs before enrolment, during the waiting period, or before the pet's first exam as pre-existing.

faqs.q: Do I need a vet exam to buy pet insurance?
faqs.a: Spot states no vet exam is needed for enrolment and has no upper age limit, with puppies and kittens 8 weeks and older eligible. Fetch covers dogs and cats 6 weeks and older and advises enrolling early so conditions are not later classed as pre-existing. For Lemonade, an enrolment exam requirement is not published on the official pages checked on 2026-09-25.

blocks.h2: How this comparison is built
blocks.html:
There is no lab test for "best pet insurance". What we can do honestly is put the figures each insurer publishes on its own website side by side, keep the condition attached to every figure, and link to the page it came from. Nothing on this page is estimated, scored or taken from a third-party comparison site.

All figures were read from the brands' own pages on 2026-09-25 and are repeated with their conditions in the fact table below. Where an official page does not publish a figure, the cell says not published on the official site instead of a guess.

The three brands quote their prices under different conditions - different deductibles, annual limits and reimbursement rates - so a raw price-to-price comparison would be misleading. That is why this page does not crown a single winner.

blocks.h2: How to choose without a fake ranking
blocks.html:
Run the same exercise the brands run themselves: request a quote for your pet on each official site, then compare the quotes you receive against each other, not against the advertised figures on this page. Advertised figures carry conditions - Spot's "from $15/month" assumes an 80% reimbursement rate, a $500 deductible, a $2,500 annual limit and a specific 2-year-old dog in ZIP 32009 - and your pet will not match those conditions exactly.

Three checks that change the outcome more than the brand name: (1) the waiting period before coverage starts - 14 days, 14 days or up to 15 days here; (2) whether a condition your pet already has counts as pre-existing - none of the three covers pre-existing conditions, though Spot publishes a 180-day symptom- and treatment-free rule for curable conditions; (3) the reimbursement percentage and deductible you choose, which move the premium more than the headline price.

Pet insurance prices are quoted, not published as a single number, so this page does two honest things: it repeats the figures each insurer puts on its own website, and it repeats the conditions those figures were calculated under - deductible, annual limit and reimbursement rate - right next to them. Nothing here is estimated, averaged across third-party comparison sites or taken from a broker ranking.

All figures were read from the brands' own pages on 2026-09-25. Where an official page does not publish a figure, the cell says not published on the official site instead of a guess.

The reason the same pet can cost $29 or $336 a month is not only the brand: it is the deductible, limit and reimbursement set chosen, the pet's breed and age, and the state. That is why every row below carries its condition.

The same-pet price check Lemonade publishes
blocks.html:
Lemonade's cost guide does something unusual: it prices one identical pet at six companies. For a 4-year-old Goldendoodle in Chicago on 80% co-insurance, the maximum annual limit and a $250 annual deductible it lists Trupanion $336, Healthy Paws $85, Fetch $99, Pets Best $77, ManyPets $73 and Lemonade $61 per month. For a 1-year-old short-haired cat in Danbury, Connecticut on a $250 deductible, 80% co-insurance, the maximum annual limit and no add-ons or discounts it lists Trupanion $58, ManyPets $44, Fetch $36, Pets Best $35 and Lemonade $29. Source: lemonade.com cost guide, checked 2026-09-25.

Treat that spread as a reminder, not a ranking: Lemonade ran the test and published it on its own page, the profiles suit its own pricing, and the page notes the companies could not be made perfectly identical (Trupanion only offered a 90% co-insurance option). The same page also publishes state averages, from $30 to $34 a month in Texas, Ohio, Pennsylvania, Georgia and Michigan up to $45 to $49 in California and Connecticut, using Lemonade's own policy rates as of October 2024.

blocks.h2: What actually moves the number
blocks.html:
Deductible. Lemonade offers $100, $250, $500, $750 or $1,000 and states plainly that a higher deductible lowers your monthly premium. Fetch says the same, and its published average assumes $300. Spot's advertised quotes assume $500 for dogs and $750 for cats. Source: lemonade.com cost guide and fetchpet.com price page, checked 2026-09-25.

Annual limit. Lemonade lets you choose anywhere from $5,000 to $100,000; Spot's advertised quotes use $2,500; Fetch's average uses $10,000. A lower limit buys a lower premium and a smaller maximum payout.

Reimbursement rate. The examples above use 80%; Spot advertises up to 90%; Fetch advertises up to 90%. Lemonade says adjusting these levels might lower your premium by 10% or 15%, and warns that it also means being covered for less when a large bill arrives.

Age, breed and state. Both Lemonade and Spot list age, breed and location as price factors, and Spot states premiums are based on your pet's current age and may increase at renewal. Entry prices on this page are therefore not quotes for an older pet.

blocks.h2: How to get a real number in three steps
blocks.html:
1. Run the same configuration at each brand: pick one deductible (say $500), one annual limit and one reimbursement rate, then take a quote for your own pet at lemonade.com, spotpet.com and fetchpet.com. Lemonade advertises a quote in as little as 90 seconds; Spot's quote entry point is its 'Click For Price' button; Fetch states its quote includes all monthly taxes and fees.

2. Compare those three quotes with each other, not with the advertised figures on this page - advertised figures carry conditions that your pet will not match exactly.

3. Check what the money buys before you pay: waiting periods (14 days illness at Lemonade and in Spot's sample policy, up to 15 days at Fetch), the deductible you chose, and whether wellness care is something you want to add on - Lemonade prices preventative packages from +$10/month and Spot prices its Platinum cat preventative add-on at $24.95/month.

faqs.q: Is Lemonade or Spot cheaper?
faqs.a: On published entry prices, Lemonade is lower for dogs ($10/month against Spot's $15/month) and Spot is lower for cats ($9/month against Lemonade's $10/month). The published averages tell a different story for dogs only: Lemonade says its policyholders pay about $48/month for dogs and about $27/month for cats, while Spot publishes no average of its own. Because Spot's advertised prices carry a $500 or $750 deductible and a $2,500 annual limit for specific pets in specific ZIP codes, the only fair comparison is two quotes for your own pet on the two official sites.

faqs.q: Which one pays claims faster?
faqs.a: Both publish a speed figure, measured differently. Lemonade says it pays 50% of eligible claims instantly through AI and pays approved claims into the bank details you enter in the app. Spot says claims are reimbursed in 48 hours or less, with most processed in under 2 business days, based on its own admin data from 2019 to 2024. Neither figure is an independent measurement, and payment still depends on the claim being covered by the policy.

faqs.q: What are the waiting periods?
faqs.a: Lemonade states 14 days for illnesses and 30 days for orthopedic conditions, with preventative package benefits usable the day after purchase. Spot's sample Accident & Illness policy states a 14-day waiting period for illness including congenital, hereditary and orthopedic illness, starting on the first effective date of coverage, and says a paid Waiting Period Health Assessment can modify it; Spot's preventative care coverage has no waiting period, so those benefits start the next day.

faqs.q: Do they cover pre-existing conditions?
faqs.a: Neither does. Lemonade treats anything your pet showed signs of before the waiting periods are up as pre-existing, while covering accidents and new illnesses as base coverage. Spot excludes pre-existing conditions but reclassifies a cured and curable condition that has been symptom-free and treatment-free for 180 days, except knee and ligament injuries.

faqs.q: Which one has better discounts?
faqs.a: Lemonade publishes a multi-pet discount whose eligibility depends on where you live, a bundle discount with other Lemonade policies, and a discount for paying annually instead of monthly. Spot publishes 10% off every pet enrolled after the first, an advertised 20% employee discount through employer benefits (up to a 10% group discount plus up to a 10% multi-pet discount on 2nd+ pets, varies by state) and Spot Perks with $2,500+ in brand discounts. Neither brand publishes a promo code page in its official sitemap, so a code you find on a third-party site is not something either brand publishes.

faqs.q: Can I use my own vet with either brand?
faqs.a: Yes in both cases. Lemonade says you can go to any vet in the United States as long as they are licensed to provide vet care in their state, and Spot says you can visit any licensed vet in the United States or Canada. Both reimburse you rather than paying the vet directly, so you settle the bill and submit the claim.

faqs.q: Which is better for an older pet?
faqs.a: Spot is the one that publishes an age policy: it covers puppies and kittens from 8 weeks old, states there is no upper age limit and no vet exam to enrol, and also states that premiums are based on your pet's current age and may increase at renewal. Lemonade does not publish a minimum or maximum enrolment age on the pages read here, so its age terms are not published on the official site.

Run the brands' own test against each other: take one configuration - a $500 deductible, an 80% reimbursement rate and a $2,500 annual limit - and request the same quote for the same pet at lemonade.com and spotpet.com. Then compare those two quotes with each other, not with the advertised figures above, because advertised figures carry conditions (Spot's dog price assumes a specific 2-year-old dog in ZIP 32009).

You pay the vet bill up front, then file; Lemonade subtracts your deductible and applies co-insurance before wiring the payout, Spot reimburses eligible expenses after your annual deductible is met, and Fetch pays you back after approval and your deductible, by direct deposit.

faqs.q: What documents do I need to submit a pet insurance claim?
faqs.a: An itemized paid invoice plus your pet's medical records. Fetch is the strictest on paper: the invoice must show a zero balance or paid in full, and it wants detailed records from the most recent checkup (SOAP notes). Spot asks for the bill and contacts your vet directly only if records are needed, though sending them may speed things up. Lemonade asks for the vet invoice or paid receipt and the records from that visit.

faqs.q: How long does reimbursement take?
faqs.a: Published speeds differ: Lemonade says 50% of eligible claims are processed instantly by AI Jim and most others within 5 business days; Spot says claims are reimbursed in 48 hrs or less; Fetch says claims are typically processed in less than 10 days, and its FAQ adds that processing typically takes within 15 days from when all documents are received. Direct deposit with Fetch is 5 to 10 days faster than paper checks.

faqs.q: Can I file a claim without an app?
faqs.a: With Lemonade, no - the official guide states the claims process is app-based. Fetch lets you file either in the app or on a computer through the member portal (Claims, then Submit a claim). Spot lets you submit the claim online through your Member Center and also publishes a claims form PDF for download.

faqs.q: What if my claim is denied?
faqs.a: Lemonade's official guidance is to review the denial explanation in the app and then appeal through the app with additional documentation from your vet. Spot requires the appeal in writing, emailed to service@customer.spotpetins.com with your reasons and supporting documents; reviews take around 30 days and the appeal window varies by state. Fetch does not publish an appeal process on its official site as of the check date.

faqs.q: Will filing a claim raise my pet insurance rate?
faqs.a: Lemonade publishes that filing claims will never result in a rate change to your Lemonade Pet policy. Neither Spot nor Fetch publishes a matching statement on its official pages as of 2026-09-25, so for those two the answer is not published on the official site - check your policy terms.

  2. Pull your pet's complete records. Ask your vet for the full file, including the date symptoms were first noted; pre-existing decisions turn on those dates, not on opinion.
  3. Write the disagreement as facts. Say why you or your vet disagree with the initial determination - that is the exact wording both Spot and Fetch require - and attach the records that back it up.

faqs.q: What is a pet insurance waiting period?
faqs.a: Spot's own definition: "A waiting period is a set period between the day you enroll and the day your coverage begins. Conditions that occur during the waiting period will be considered pre-existing and will not be eligible for coverage under your plan." Fetch words it as the gap between enrollment and when coverage kicks in, and Lemonade calls it the time the insurer requires you to wait until your pet is eligible for reimbursement on specific conditions (all checked 2026-09-28).

faqs.q: How long is the waiting period with Lemonade?
faqs.a: 0 days for accidents, 14 days for illnesses and 30 days for orthopedic conditions, counted from the policy's start date. Preventive care from a preventative package can be used the day after purchase. That is the whole national table Lemonade publishes - no state-by-state version appears on the pages cited here (checked 2026-09-28).

faqs.q: How long is the waiting period with Spot?
faqs.a: Spot says its plans "typically" have a 14-day waiting period and then points you at the sample policy for your state's specific waiting periods. Of the six state Accident & Illness samples read on 2026-09-28 (AZ, CA, CO, FL, GA, IL), five state 14 days covering accidents, illnesses and ligament and knee conditions; the California sample states 14 days for illness only and adds a paid Waiting Period Health Assessment that can waive it. Preventive care add-ons start the next day.

faqs.q: How long is the waiting period with Fetch?
faqs.a: Up to 15 days for accident and illness coverage combined, beginning the day after you enroll, plus a separate 6-month waiting period before orthopedic conditions - hip dysplasia, elbow dysplasia, luxating patella, IVDD and ruptured cruciate ligaments are named. Fetch Wellness has no waiting period. Fetch also publishes a knee waiver: a vet exam within 180 days of enrollment with SOAP notes sent in your first claim (checked 2026-09-28).

faqs.q: Do waiting periods change from state to state?
faqs.a: For Spot, yes - that is what its FAQ means by "see our sample policy for more information on your states specific waiting periods": spotpet.com/sample-policy hosts separate Accident Only and Accident & Illness sample PDFs per state, and the sentences are not identical (the California sample has no separate accident sentence and offers a waiver the others do not). Fetch does not publish a state table but disclaims that waiting periods vary by state or province. The two Lemonade pages read print one national table only (checked 2026-09-28).

faqs.q: Can you shorten or waive a pet insurance waiting period?
faqs.a: Fetch publishes a way for knees: have your pet examined by a vet within 180 days of enrollment to show no relevant pre-existing conditions, then submit that visit's SOAP notes with your first claim. Spot's California sample policy offers a paid Waiting Period Health Assessment (exam 3 days before or 7 days after the effective date, form returned within 30 days) that waives the wait to the effective date or the day after the exam, whichever is later. The Lemonade pages cited here publish no such option (checked 2026-09-28).

faqs.q: What happens if my pet gets sick during the waiting period?
faqs.a: All three treat it as pre-existing: Fetch says any accident, injury or illness during the wait "will be considered a pre-existing condition, which means it won't be eligible for coverage"; Spot's sample policy says any condition occurring during a waiting period is a pre-existing condition; Lemonade says anything your pet showed signs of before the wait ended counts as pre-existing. Spot adds that a curable pre-existing condition can count as new after 180 days symptom- and treatment-free, except chronic and ligament/knee conditions in the samples read (checked 2026-09-28).

faqs.q: Do wellness and preventive add-ons have a waiting period?
faqs.a: No, according to all three brands' own pages: Fetch Wellness claims work "on or after the effective date" in your enrollment email; Spot says preventive care has no deductible or waiting period and starts the next day; Lemonade says preventative care coverage kicks in on the effective date (its product page says the day after purchase). The base accident and illness waits above still apply (checked 2026-09-28).

faqs.q: Does switching insurers restart the waiting periods?
faqs.a: Yes - that is the coverage gap Lemonade defines in its own glossary: "A period when switching providers where your pet may temporarily lack full coverage, since new waiting periods apply with each new policy." Spot's California sample policy says the same thing for a new enrollment: "A new enrollment will result in new waiting periods", and conditions before it are pre-existing. This is why switching mid-treatment can cost coverage (checked 2026-09-28).

blocks.h2: How this page was checked
blocks.html:
On 2026-09-28 we read the pages each brand itself publishes on waiting periods, not review sites or comparison tables:

  • Lemonade - its waiting-period guide (page marked Last Updated: Jun 3, 2026) and the FAQ on its pet insurance product page.
  • Spot - the FAQ block on its home page, its dog insurance page, and six Accident & Illness sample policies linked from spotpet.com/sample-policy: Arizona, California, Colorado, Florida, Georgia and Illinois (plus Arizona's Accident Only sample). The five non-California forms repeat the same waiting-period sentence; California's does not.
  • Fetch - its "What is a waiting period for pet insurance?" FAQ, its "Is there a waiting period for pet wellness?" FAQ, and the disclaimer on its home page.

Where a brand does not publish a figure - or does not publish one state by state - this page says so instead of filling the gap with a third-party estimate.

Only Spot puts this in writing. Its FAQ ends with "See our sample policy for more information on your state's specific waiting periods", and Spot's sample-policy page publishes a separate Accident Only and Accident & Illness PDF for each state. Reading six of them on 2026-09-28 shows what that means in practice: five states carry the identical sentence (14 days covering accidents, illnesses and ligament and knee conditions), while California's form covers 14 days of illness only - including congenital, hereditary and orthopedic illness - and offers a paid Waiting Period Health Assessment that the other forms do not mention.

faqs.q: Why do Lemonade and Fetch publish competitor prices that disagree about who is cheaper?
faqs.a: Because each one prices a different pet under a different policy. Fetch prices a 1-year-old small mixed breed in Tampa, FL 33602 at a $5,000 limit, $500 deductible and 80% reimbursement, without wellness, "as of March 2026". Lemonade prices a 4-year-old Goldendoodle in Chicago at a $250 deductible, 80% co-insurance and the maximum annual limit, with no date on the competitor rows. Same two brands, opposite order - the assumption footnote is the difference.

faqs.q: What does Spot's "Starting from $15/mo" actually assume?
faqs.a: Spot's footnote spells it out: an accident and illness plan with an 80% reimbursement rate, a $500 annual deductible and a $2,500 annual limit, for a 2-year-old small mixed dog of 11-25 lbs in ZIP 32009, advertised as of Dec. 11 2024. The cat version uses a $750 deductible and ZIP 33801. Your ZIP, your pet's age and a different deductible all move that number.

faqs.q: Why doesn't Fetch publish a starting price?
faqs.a: It publishes averages instead: $35/month for dogs and $22/month for cats under a stated $10,000 limit / $300 deductible / 80% reimbursement configuration for 07.01.2024-06.30.2025, plus twelve breed averages from its own in-force policies. The page says your price depends on age, breed and location, so it gives portfolio figures rather than a floor.

faqs.q: How old are the prices on this page?
faqs.a: Each brand dates its own figures differently: Lemonade marks its guide "Last Updated: Jun 3, 2026" while the underlying premium analysis and state table are "as of October, 2024"; Spot dates its advertised premium "Dec. 11 2024"; Fetch dates its comparison "as of March 2026", its averages 07.01.2024-06.30.2025 and its breed figures 01.01.25-11.01.25. All three pages were read again on 2026-09-28.

faqs.q: Are the three brands' published prices comparable?
faqs.a: No. Lemonade's averages come from its own policyholders across ages, breeds and locations; Spot's starting prices are one fixed plan for one age, weight band and ZIP; Fetch's averages use the most common configuration of $10,000 limit, $300 deductible and 80% reimbursement. Subtracting one from another tells you about the assumptions, not about the brands.

faqs.q: Do these published prices include taxes, fees and add-ons?
faqs.a: Fetch states its comparison premiums "do not include any taxes or fees" and that Lemonade and Pets Best pricing excludes the optional Exam Fee add-on. Spot's advertised premium is a specific accident and illness configuration, and its other discounts (10% multi-pet, 20% employee) are listed separately. Lemonade's figures assume no add-ons or discounts.

faqs.q: What is the actual price I would pay?
faqs.a: The quote each brand gives you for your pet - Lemonade's quote flow, Spot's "Click For Price" button and Fetch's "Get your price" button. The published numbers on this page are averages, floors and worked examples stamped with someone else's pet, ZIP and deductible (read 2026-09-28).

faqs.q: Do the brands update these published prices?
faqs.a: Only by rewriting the page. Each price carries whatever stamp the brand gave it (Jun 3 2026 / October 2024, Dec. 11 2024, March 2026), so a figure can sit on an official page for months after the analysis behind it. Re-reading the page - as this page does, most recently on 2026-09-28 - is the only way to know what is printed today.

blocks.h2: How this page was checked
blocks.html:
On 2026-09-28 we read three pages - and only official pages - looking for every monthly price each brand publishes, together with the assumption footnote the brand prints underneath it:

  • Lemonade - its pet insurance cost guide (page marked Last Updated: Jun 3, 2026): starting price, species averages, the Goldendoodle and Danbury worked examples, the two six-insurer tables and the 47-state range table.
  • Spot - the home page: the two "Starting from" prices in the hero and plan cards, their ^ and ^^ footnotes, the $12,345 claim example and its $75.01/month policy footnote.
  • Fetch - fetchpet.com/pet-insurance-cost: the species averages, the twelve breed averages, the four-insurer comparison table and the three methodology footnotes at the bottom of the page.

No third-party comparison site, review site or broker table was used. Where a brand does not publish a figure, this page says "not published on the official site" instead of borrowing an estimate from somewhere else, and every cell in the table below links the page it came from.

blocks.h2: Two brands print each other's prices
Side by side: every price each brand publishes
The two competitor tables disagree - on purpose
blocks.html:
This is the part of "pet insurance cost by brand" that comparison sites skip. Two of the three brands price their rivals themselves, and the two tables put the same companies in opposite order:

  • Fetch's table (as of March 2026): Fetch $27.51, Spot $19.79, Pets Best $21.91, Lemonade $14.97 - so on this quote Lemonade is the cheapest of the four and Fetch the most expensive.
  • Lemonade's table (competitor rows undated): Trupanion $336, Fetch $99, Healthy Paws $85, Pets Best $77, ManyPets $73, Lemonade $61 - so on this quote Fetch is more than 50% dearer than Lemonade.

Both are published by the brand itself, on its own domain, and neither is wrong: they are answers to different questions. Fetch prices a 1-year-old small mixed breed in Tampa at a $5,000 limit, $500 deductible and 80% reimbursement with no wellness; Lemonade prices a 4-year-old Goldendoodle in Chicago at a $250 deductible, 80% co-insurance and the maximum annual limit. Change the pet, the deductible and the limit, and the ranking flips. That is exactly why this page stamps every figure with the page it came from, the assumption it carries and the date we read it - and why any sentence that starts "Brand A is cheaper than Brand B" needs the assumption attached to be worth anything.

blocks.h2: The date stamp is the whole point
blocks.html:
Every brand dates its prices, but they date different things. Lemonade dates the page (Jun 3, 2026) and the analysis behind its averages (October, 2024) - the competitor rows in between carry no date at all. Spot dates only the advertised starting premium (Dec. 11 2024), and only on the dog footnote. Fetch dates everything: the comparison (March 2026), the species averages (07.01.2024-06.30.2025), the breed averages (01.01.25-11.01.25) and its own site statistics (9.10.2026).

So a price printed today can rest on an analysis that is 11, 17 or 20 months old. That is not a scandal - insurers cannot publish live rates - but it means the honest way to state a figure is number + assumption + brand's own date + the day you read it, which is the format every row and fact above uses.

faqs.q: Which pet insurance wellness add-on pays the most per item?

Spot's Platinum endorsement sums to $450 and Lemonade prints no dollar caps at all. Those are published ceilings, not quotes - what you pay depends on your state, your pet and your declarations page.

faqs.q: Do wellness add-ons have a waiting period?
faqs.a: Lemonade says no waiting period for preventative care - coverage activates at 12:01 AM the day after purchase. Fetch says no waiting period for wellness either, with claims accepted from the effective date in the enrollment confirmation email. Spot's sample preventive-care endorsement states no wellness waiting period of its own. faqs.q: Can I buy a wellness plan on its own, without pet insurance?

Fetch combines them too at $175 / $200 / $250 a year. Lemonade pays routine dental prophylaxis up to $150 a year only in Preventative+ - Routine Vet Care Plus explicitly excludes routine cleanings - while spay/neuter sits in Routine Vet Care Plus and the Puppy/Kitten package (read 2026-09-28).

Spot's wellness page advertises microchip implantation coverage included, but neither of the two sample preventive-care endorsements we read on 2026-09-28 contains a microchip line.

faqs.q: Can I just add up the per-item caps to see what a plan pays?

faqs.q: How do I check the schedule that applies to my own policy?
faqs.a: Read your declarations page and the endorsement attached to it - Spot's sample endorsement says outright that it pays only for procedures listed for the Preventive Care option on your declarations page, and both Fetch and Nationwide say plans vary by state. Spot also publishes state sample policies at spotpet.com/sample-policy, which is where the Gold and Platinum schedules on this page come from (read 2026-09-28).

On 2026-09-28 we opened four official sources - and nothing else - looking for published dollar figures attached to individual wellness items:

• The line items themselves are not the same shape. Spot and Nationwide each pay dental cleaning and spay/neuter out of one combined line, so a pet that only needs a cleaning is drawing from the same pot as one that needs a surgery. Fetch also combines them. Lemonade is the opposite: dental lives in Preventative+ only, spay/neuter lives in two other packages, so no single Lemonade package covers both.
  • Only two brands print a ceiling you can plan around. Fetch and Nationwide publish plan-level totals; Spot publishes per-item maximums and no total; Lemonade publishes counts and an annual limit it does not quantify. Anything that ranks these four on price is comparing a ceiling with a list.
  • An item's published cap can be zero. Spot's Gold endorsement prints $0.00 for heartworm/flea prevention, health certificate, urinalysis, blood test and the Bordetella vaccine - the line exists, the maximum is zero. Nationwide's $450 plan prints Not covered for the extra test and for spay/neuter or dental cleaning. A checklist that only asks whether an item is listed would call both of those covered.

The printed caps sum to $550, $805 and $1,200 against printed ceilings of $390, $700 and $1,200; Nationwide's columns do sum to $450 and $800. articles.h1: How long do you have to file a pet insurance claim? The three official windows

faqs.q: How long do I have to file a claim with Spot?
faqs.a: Spot's own FAQ answer is 270 days: you can submit a claim within 270 days from the date of treatment. Spot's sample Accident & Illness policy prints the same 270 days and calls it the date of service. Both were read on 2026-09-28.

faqs.q: Does Lemonade give me 180 days to file?
faqs.a: Yes - Lemonade's claim guide says you file through the app within 180 days of treatment, and it presents that as a condition of the claim being eligible for coverage. The same page says a Lemonade Pet policy in Texas has 90 days to file a claim.

faqs.q: How long after the vet visit can I file with Fetch?
faqs.a: 90 days. Fetch's claims page says claims must be submitted within 90 days of the vet visit to be eligible for reimbursement, and that claims submitted after 90 days won't be covered. Its claim FAQ gives the same 90 days counted from your pet's treatment.

faqs.q: Does the clock start on the day of the accident?
faqs.a: Not on any of the pages we read. Spot's sample policy counts its 270 days from the date of service, Lemonade counts from the date of treatment and Fetch counts from the vet visit - so the window starts when your pet is treated, and the paperwork (invoice, records) has to be finished inside that same window.

faqs.q: What happens if I file after the deadline?
faqs.a: Fetch is the only one of the three that writes the consequence out: claims submitted after 90 days won't be covered. Spot's sample policy says you must submit within 270 days, and Lemonade frames the 180 days as a condition of eligibility for coverage.

faqs.q: Do some states get a shorter window?
faqs.a: Yes for Lemonade: its claim guide states that a Lemonade Pet policy in Texas has 90 days to file a claim instead of 180. Spot and Fetch publish no state variation in the filing window on the pages we read - Spot does publish state variation for its appeal deadline, which is a different clock.

faqs.q: How fast does Spot pay a claim?
faqs.a: Spot's homepage prints claims reimbursed in 48 hrs or less, and it emails you when the claim is received, when it needs more information and when it is complete. The homepage text does not say what moment the 48 hours is measured from.

faqs.q: How long does Fetch take to process a claim?
faqs.a: Fetch's claim submission FAQ says claims are typically processed within 15 days from when we receive all your documents, and that direct deposit pays you back 5 to 10 days faster than a check. Its claims page separately prints under 10 days - two official figures from one brand, reported as published.

faqs.q: How do I appeal a denied claim?
faqs.a: Spot's route is a written appeal by email to service@customer.spotpetins.com with your reasons and supporting documents; it says the number of days to appeal varies by the state your policy was issued in and that reviews take around 30 days. Lemonade tells you to appeal in the app with extra documentation from your vet. Fetch publishes no appeal route on the pages we read.

faqs.q: Does Nationwide publish a filing deadline?
faqs.a: No. Its public FAQ explains how to file a claim in three steps and says most plans start 1-14 days after your application is approved, but it prints no number of days for filing a claim. We read that page on 2026-09-28 specifically looking for one and found none.

blocks.h2: How this page was checked
blocks.html:
On 2026-09-28 we opened the official pages that publish a filing deadline - and nothing else - looking for a number of days and the sentence around it:

  • Lemonade - its claim guide (how to file a pet insurance claim), which carries the 180-day window, the Texas exception, the document list, the AI speed figures and the in-app appeal route.
  • Spot - its FAQ page (the 270-day answer, the appeal rules, the status emails), its homepage (48 hrs or less) and two of its own sample Accident & Illness policy forms - California and Arizona - which print the 270 days as a contract sentence.
  • Fetch - its claims page (90 days and the 'won't be covered' sentence, under 10 days, direct deposit), its 'when can I submit' FAQ and its claim submission document FAQ (zero-balance invoice, 15 days from all documents in hand).
  • Nationwide (petinsurance.com) - its public FAQ, checked specifically to see whether a fourth brand publishes a filing deadline. It does not, so no number appears for it here.

No figure on this page comes from a broker, a review site or a comparison chart. Where a brand prints nothing - a state exception, an appeal window, an appeal route - the table says not published on the official site instead of filling the cell from somewhere else.

blocks.h2: Three windows, and two clocks that run after them
The three filing windows, side by side - official published figures only
Where the three windows disagree
blocks.html:
• The spread is three to one. 270 days at Spot against 90 days at Fetch - the same product category, the same reimbursement model, and a 180-day difference in how long you can wait before the paperwork has to be in.
  • All three start the clock at the treatment, not at the incident. Spot's sample policy says date of service, Lemonade says date of treatment, Fetch says the vet visit. Nothing we read starts the count on the day the accident happened, so the window is about getting the invoice and the records filed, not about noticing a symptom late.
  • Only one brand spells out the penalty. Fetch prints that claims submitted after 90 days won't be covered. Spot's sample policy uses the word must. Lemonade phrases it as eligibility for coverage. Three different levels of bluntness for the same kind of rule.
  • One brand contains a second deadline inside it. Lemonade prints 180 days for the general case and 90 days for Texas policies on the same page - a reader who only skims the headline number will have the wrong deadline in one state.
  • A brand's FAQ and its own contract can use different words. Spot's FAQ says 270 days from the date of treatment; Spot's sample policy says 270 days from the date of service. We quote both, and we do not choose one for them.
  • The paperwork is on the same clock. Fetch's zero-balance invoice and the records from the most recent checkup both have to exist inside its 90 days, and Lemonade needs a record from within 12 months of the policy start - which is why a first claim often waits on the vet's office rather than on the insurer.

blocks.h2: The second clock: what happens after you file
blocks.html:
Filing deadlines are one number; the wait afterwards is another, and the three brands measure different things by different units. Spot prints a payout claim (48 hrs or less) without saying what moment its clock starts from. Lemonade publishes a processing mix (50% instant via its AI, most others within 5 business days) and warns that complex claims take longer. Fetch publishes two processing figures: under 10 days on its claims page, and within 15 days from when it receives all your documents in its claim submission FAQ. Both were read on the same day. We show both figures and both sources rather than picking the one that reads better.

One more asymmetry: only Spot publishes an appeal deadline at all, and even then it is not a fixed number - the days to appeal vary by the state that issued the policy, the appeal goes in writing, and Spot says reviews take around 30 days. Lemonade routes appeals through the app without a day count, and Fetch's official pages describe no appeal route.

faqs.q: How long is the waiting period with GEICO?
faqs.a: GEICO does not say. Its guide answers the question with "ask an agent what waiting periods apply to your policy", and its landing page only defines pre-existing conditions in terms of the waiting period. The day counts exist one step away: GEICO's footer links to Embrace's terms, where the sample contract for 48 states and DC has no accident wait, a 14-day illness wait and a 180-day orthopedic exclusion list, and the Kansas, New Mexico and South Carolina contract says two days accident, fourteen days illness and six months orthopedic for dogs (all read 2026-09-29).

faqs.q: How long is the waiting period with Allstate?
faqs.a: "All policies have a 2-week illness waiting period. Other waiting periods and exclusions vary by state." That is the whole published answer: no accident figure, no orthopedic figure, no cruciate figure and no cancer figure appear on the Allstate pet insurance pages read 2026-09-29. Its footer links to the same Embrace terms GEICO links to.

faqs.q: How long is the waiting period with ASPCA?
faqs.a: Its quote page prints a five-row table: accidents and injuries excluding ligament and knee injuries - no waiting period; preventive care - no waiting period; ligament and knee injuries - 14 days; illnesses - 14 days; hereditary and congenital conditions - 14 days. The same page's effective-date text then says accident and illness coverage begins 14 days after the effective date, so accidents are published as both 0 and 14 days on one page (read 2026-09-29).

faqs.q: Where do GEICO's and Allstate's day counts actually live?
faqs.a: In one document neither of them hosts. Both footers say the product is administered by Embrace Pet Insurance Agency and underwritten by American Modern Insurance Group companies, then point to embracepetinsurance.com/coverage/embrace-terms for full terms and conditions. That terms page publishes two versions: V5 for Kansas, New Mexico and South Carolina (2 days accident, 14 days illness, 6 months orthopedic for dogs) and V6 for the other 48 states and DC (no accident wait, 14 days illness, 180-day orthopedic exclusion list) (read 2026-09-29).

faqs.q: How long before cancer is covered?
faqs.a: No brand publishes a cancer-specific wait, so the illness wait is what applies. In the Embrace contract behind GEICO and Allstate, cancer is named inside "Illnesses" - fourteen days - with two written traps: an undiagnosed mass before the end of that wait is not covered "including those caused by cancer", and osteosarcoma showing signs during the orthopedic period is excluded. Allstate files cancer under illnesses, so its 2-week figure applies. ASPCA lists cancer under illness coverage, so its 14-day row applies (all read 2026-09-29).

faqs.q: How long is the cruciate ligament (CCL or TPLO) waiting period?
faqs.a: In the Embrace contract GEICO and Allstate link to, a cruciate ligament injury showing signs in the first 180 days after the start date is excluded and pre-existing for the life of the policy (V6, 48 states and DC), while the V5 form for KS, NM and SC uses a six-month orthopedic waiting period instead - reducible by an orthopedic exam in states that allow it. ASPCA publishes 14 days for "Ligament and knee injuries" on its quote page, but its California notice prints 12 months for ligament and knee conditions on the Levels 2, 3 and 4 disclosure (all read 2026-09-29).

faqs.q: Do waiting periods change from state to state?
faqs.a: For all three, yes - in three different ways. Allstate just says they "vary by state". The Embrace contract GEICO and Allstate link to splits into two versions: V5 for KS, NM and SC and V6 for the other 48 states and DC, and the accident wait is 2 days in the first and none in the second. ASPCA publishes state-by-state documents - sample plans, an Insurer Disclosure of Important Policy Provisions and a Waiting Period Waiver Form per state - plus a California notice with three different waiting-period sets (read 2026-09-29).

faqs.q: Can you shorten or waive a pet insurance waiting period?
faqs.a: Two of the three publish a route. Embrace's orthopedic exam and waiver process can cut the orthopedic wait "to as few as 14 days" in states that allow it - an exam inside the first 14 days moves the end date to the end of the illness wait, a later exam moves it to the exam date. ASPCA links a state-specific Waiting Period Waiver Form and a Waiting Period Health Assessment from its state documents page. GEICO's own pages publish no waiver; Allstate's publish none either (all read 2026-09-29).

faqs.q: Does the waiting period restart later on?
faqs.a: In the contract behind GEICO and Allstate, yes on a coverage increase: the waiting period "also applies again when there are Coverage increases but is waived for policy renewals and optional Coverage renewals". ASPCA's quote page does not publish a restart rule; it only says conditions during the wait are ineligible. Switching insurers still means a fresh wait with the new company (read 2026-09-29).

blocks.h2: How this page was checked
blocks.html:
On 2026-09-29 we read the pages each brand itself publishes about waiting periods, plus the contract documents those pages point to:

  • GEICO - its pet insurance landing page (footer disclaimer included) and its flagship guide, which was bylined August 31, 2026.
  • Allstate - the pet insurance landing page with its FAQ block and footnotes, and its dog insurance resource page for how it classifies cancer.
  • ASPCA - the quote page with its waiting-period table and effective-date sections, the What's Covered page, the California policy notice and the state documents page. Direct requests to that domain return 403, so those four pages were read through a text-rendering fetch of the same URLs on 2026-09-29.
  • Embrace terms - the terms page with its state selector, and both live sample contracts (V5 and V6), because GEICO's and Allstate's own footers link there for "full terms and conditions".

Where a brand does not publish a figure, this page says so instead of filling the gap with a third-party estimate.

blocks.h2: Side by side: what each brand's own pages say
Every published day count, charted
GEICO and Allstate both point at the same contract
blocks.html:
Neither GEICO nor Allstate underwrites its own pet insurance, and neither prints a waiting-period day count of its own - GEICO's guide hands the question to an agent, Allstate's FAQ gives one number and defers the rest to the states. Both sites then say the same thing in their footer: administered by Embrace Pet Insurance Agency, underwritten by American Modern Insurance Group companies, and "For full terms and conditions, visit www.embracepetinsurance.com/coverage/embrace-terms".

That terms page publishes the contract in two live versions, chosen by a state dropdown: V5 for Kansas, New Mexico and South Carolina (two days accident, fourteen days illness, six months orthopedic for dogs) and V6 for the other 48 states and DC (no accident wait, fourteen days illness, and a 180-day exclusion that attaches cruciate ligament disease, IVDD, patellar luxation and hip dysplasia to the policy for life if they show up early). The accident answer therefore differs by state: 0 days in most of the country, 2 days in three states.

Cancer gets no separate line in any of this: the contract names cancer inside "Illnesses", so the fourteen-day illness wait is the number, with two written traps - an undiagnosed mass before the end of that wait is not covered even when cancer caused it, and osteosarcoma that shows up inside the orthopedic period is excluded.

blocks.h2: ASPCA publishes a table - and two different accident answers
blocks.html:
ASPCA is the only one of the three that prints day counts on its own site, and the table is genuinely useful: no waiting period for accidents (excluding ligament and knee injuries), no waiting period for preventive care, and 14 days each for ligament and knee injuries, illnesses, and hereditary and congenital conditions.

Then the same page undercuts its own first row: the effective-date section states that "Coverage for accidents and illnesses begins 14 days after your coverage effective date" and that anything happening inside those 14 days is ineligible. Both statements were read on 2026-09-29 and neither references the other.

The state paperwork goes further than the marketing pages: ASPCA's California notice prints three waiting-period sets on one page - 30-day illness plus a 180-day hereditary window plus a 12-month ligament-and-knee wait for Levels 2, 3 and 4; a 14-day illness and 14-day ligament wait for Complete Coverage; and a 14-day accident-and-illness and 14-day ligament set on a third form. The page does not say which form a given reader is sold.

blocks.h2: State by state, in plain terms
blocks.html:
All three say waiting periods vary by state - and each one proves it differently. Allstate says it in one sentence and stops. The Embrace contract behind GEICO and Allstate publishes two versions and lets you pick your state from a dropdown to see which one you get. ASPCA publishes per-state sample plans, an Insurer Disclosure of Important Policy Provisions and, where it applies, a Waiting Period Waiver Form, and links a Waiting Period Health Assessment.

Practical consequence: any single "GEICO waiting period" number you read on a comparison site is at best a summary of one of two contract versions, and comparison sites do not usually say which. The contract you are sold - and the state you live in - decides.

blocks.h2: The same table for Lemonade, Spot and Fetch
blocks.html: We already read this field for the three brands we track most closely: pet insurance waiting periods compared covers Lemonade's 0 / 14 / 30 days, Spot's 14-day state sample policies and Fetch's up-to-15-day plus 6-month orthopedic wait, with the same source-per-cell discipline used here. The two pages are meant to be read together: one answers "what do the brands on this site publish", the other answers "what do GEICO, ASPCA and Allstate publish".
